body:
You do not need an engineering degree to vape, but a little electrical knowledge helps you choose hardware, set it up sensibly and understand what product pages mean. Ohms, watts and volts are the three words you will meet most often, and they describe how electricity behaves in your device. This guide explains each one in plain language, how they relate through two simple formulas, worked examples with real numbers, typical ranges for different styles, how to set up and adjust power, what goes wrong when settings are off and how to use the right battery. It is written for adults aged 21 and over. Nicotine is addictive, and this is general information, not a manual for any specific device. Always follow the manufacturer's instructions.

## Ohms: resistance
Ohms, written with the Greek letter omega (Ω), measure how much a coil resists the flow of current. Low-resistance coils draw more current and heat faster. High-resistance coils heat more gently. Think of a water pipe: a wide pipe lets a lot of water through and a narrow one restricts it. Resistance is the narrowness of the pipe. A coil's resistance is printed on the coil or the pod, for example 0.6 Ω or 1.2 Ω.

## Volts: electrical pressure
Volts (V) describe the electrical pressure that pushes current through the coil. A fully charged lithium-ion battery is about 4.2 volts and a discharged one about 3.0, with 3.7 volts as the nominal value. Some devices let you set voltage directly, but many convert it for you to deliver a chosen wattage. Think of volts as the water pressure in the pipe.

## Watts: power
Watts (W) measure the power the device sends to the coil. More watts means more heat, more vapor and faster liquid use. Every coil has a recommended wattage range, and staying within it protects both flavor and lifespan. Too low and the vapor is weak and cool. Too high and the liquid can scorch and the coil can burn out. Think of watts as how much water per second comes out of the pipe, which is the useful work.

## How they relate
Two formulas tie them together. Power in watts equals voltage squared divided by resistance in ohms (P = V² / R). And current in amps equals voltage divided by resistance (I = V / R). In practice, you pick a coil with a resistance suited to your style and set the wattage within its range, and the device works out the voltage it needs.

### Worked examples
- **3.7 V across a 0.5 Ω coil:** power is 3.7 × 3.7 / 0.5 = 27.4 W, and current is 3.7 / 0.5 = 7.4 A. That is a lot of current, so the battery must be able to supply it.
- **3.7 V across a 1.0 Ω coil:** power is 13.7 W, and current is 3.7 A.
- **3.7 V across a 1.5 Ω coil:** power is about 9.1 W, and current is about 2.5 A.
- **To get 15 W from a 0.8 Ω coil:** voltage needed is the square root of (15 × 0.8), which is the square root of 12, about 3.46 V.

You do not have to do these sums, because the device does them, but they show why a low-resistance coil needs a battery that can supply high current, and why higher resistance coils suit smaller batteries.

## Typical ranges
- **MTL coils:** about 1 ohm or higher, at lower wattage, commonly 8 to 20 watts. They give a tighter draw, and suit nicotine salts and pods.
- **Sub-ohm coils:** below 1 ohm, at higher wattage, commonly 20 to 80 watts or more. They give a more open draw and a lot of vapor, and suit low-strength freebase liquids.

See [sub-ohm versus mouth-to-lung](/blog/sub-ohm-vs-mouth-to-lung/) for how the two styles compare.

## Start low
Begin at the lower end of the recommended range and increase gradually. If the vapor tastes harsh or burnt, lower the power. If it feels cool or weak, raise it in small steps, such as a watt or two at a time. Most coils list a range, such as 15 to 25 watts, and the best setting is often near the middle for a new coil. A new coil also needs priming before you vape. See [how to prime a new coil or pod](/blog/how-to-prime-a-new-coil-or-pod/).

## Why the wrong settings cause problems
- **Too much power for the coil:** the liquid scorches, the cotton burns and the coil wears quickly. You get a burnt taste.
- **Too little power:** the coil does not heat enough, so vapor is thin and the liquid may pool, causing gurgling.
- **Liquid too thick for the power:** the coil dries out because it cannot wick fast enough.
- **Liquid too thin for the power:** the coil floods and leaks.

See [dry hits explained](/blog/dry-hits-explained/) and [why a vape tastes burnt](/blog/vape-tastes-burnt/).

## Battery and current
A low-resistance coil at high power draws a lot of current, so the battery must be rated to supply it. Batteries have a continuous discharge rating, in amps, and using a battery with too low a rating for your setup can make it overheat. That is why removable batteries must be matched to the device and bought from reputable sources. See [lithium battery care basics](/blog/lithium-battery-care-basics-for-vapes/). If you use a sealed device or a pod, the maker has already matched battery and coil, and you do not need to calculate anything.

## Common mistakes
- **Ignoring the coil's recommended range.**
- **Setting power by the highest number the device allows.**
- **Using a coil with the wrong resistance for your style.**
- **Mixing battery types or ages in a multi-battery device.**
- **Assuming that more watts is always better.**

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Do I need to know this for a disposable?
No. A disposable has everything matched by the maker. This knowledge matters for refillable and adjustable devices.

### What is a smart or temperature-control device?
Some devices adjust power automatically or limit temperature. They still depend on the same electrical relationships, and you should follow the manufacturer's instructions.

### Why do pods not show watts?
Many pods run at a fixed output chosen by the maker, so there is nothing to set.

### Can I use any coil in any tank?
No. Coils fit specific tanks and have specific ranges. Match the model.

### Why does my device show a different resistance from the coil?
Small differences come from measurement and the connection. A large difference can mean a poor connection or a damaged coil.

## Shop
Browse [vape kits](/shop/vape-kits/) and [coils and pods](/shop/coils-pods/). All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## A step-by-step setup example
You have a tank with a 0.4 ohm mesh coil rated for 40 to 70 watts, and a mod that lets you set watts. Start at 45 watts, near the low end. Prime the coil by adding liquid, letting it soak for several minutes and taking a few gentle puffs at a lower power, such as 30 watts. Then set 45 watts, and take a few puffs. If the vapor feels cool or thin, raise the power by 2 or 3 watts and try again. If it tastes harsh, lower it. After a few adjustments, you will find a setting that suits your taste, usually well within the range. Write it down, or use the device's memory, so you can return to it.

## Safety margins for batteries
Removable cells have a continuous discharge rating. For a 0.4 ohm coil at 3.7 volts, current is about 9.25 amps, so a battery rated at 15 amps or more gives a comfortable margin. A battery rated at 8 amps would be pushed beyond its limit. Using a battery with too low a rating is one of the most common causes of problems in advanced devices. If you are not sure, choose a higher rating, from a reputable source, and follow the manufacturer's guidance.

## Understanding the numbers on a coil
A coil may be printed with something like "0.4 Ω, 40 to 70 W". The first number is the resistance. The second is the recommended power range. Some coils also state the type, such as mesh, and the maker's suggested liquid. These details tell you how it is meant to be used. A coil used outside its range wears quickly or performs badly.

## Keeping the electrical side simple
If you find all of this daunting, choose a pod device or a disposable, where the maker has set everything. You can enjoy vaping without ever thinking about ohms. If you later move to an adjustable device, the ideas here will make the transition easier, and the formulas will help you check that a setup makes sense.

## A quick reference table in words
A 0.3 ohm coil usually works around 50 to 100 watts and suits a large tank with open airflow. A 0.6 ohm coil often runs around 25 to 50 watts. A 1.0 ohm coil often runs around 12 to 25 watts and suits a tighter draw. A 1.5 ohm or higher coil often runs around 8 to 15 watts and suits pods. These are rough, and the coil's own rating is what counts, but they show how resistance and power go together.
